issues.explanation: Occupation 'Retired' is implausible for age 28 (retired is implausible if age < 50).

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits awkwardly with 'my memories are very clear and detailed' and 'mostly pictures or images' for a PTSD profile tied to a life-threatening accident; this pattern suggests unusually easy verbal processing despite vivid intrusive-style memory, which weakens coherence of the memory node.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking whether someone is following him implies an interpersonal pursuit/assault-type danger theme, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being a life-threatening accident and with the rest of the profile, which does not otherwise indicate persecution-related threat.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' also implies an interpersonal harm/blame theme that does not fit well with the accident trauma context or the other selected appraisals, memories, and threats.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Restricting food as a coping strategy is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other items describe accident-related sensory threat (loud sounds, startle), image-based trauma memory, and self-critical appraisals, with maladaptive responses centered on avoidance/removal from reminders and rumination/meaning seeking. Undereating introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, making it the least clinically coherent item in this five-component profile.

vignette:
Carl, a 52-year-old film director, had always been known for his ability to create compelling narratives, but his own life had taken a dark turn after a life-threatening accident that had left him feeling as though he were living in a story he no longer recognized. The incident occurred during a routine shoot in a remote location; while setting up a scene, an equipment malfunction caused a heavy rig to fall, narrowly missing him but injuring one of his crew members. The shock and fear of that moment had ingrained itself deeply in his mind, manifesting in vivid, haunting memories that replayed like a poorly edited film reel, filled with images of panic and chaos. These memories distorted his self-perception, leading Carl to think that if he had been a better director, the accident wouldn't have happened, reinforcing his belief that he was somehow fundamentally flawed. Once the memories took hold, they made Carl feel as though the threat of that day had never truly passed; the chaos felt like a lingering shadow that haunted him, shifting his perception of safety in everyday situations. Once these memories surfaced, they heightened his sense of threat, making him feel as though the chaos of that day was still a looming presence in his life. Once these memories surfaced, they transformed into a looming sense of threat, as Carl could not shake the feeling that the danger of that day had re-emerged, as if the chaos were still present in his life. These memories were so clear that he often found himself unable to articulate the emotions attached to them, trapped in a cycle where words failed him, leaving him feeling isolated in his anguish. Once these memories surfaced, they transformed into a looming sense of threat, as Carl could not shake the feeling that the danger of that day had re-emerged, as if the chaos were still present in his life.

In the months following the accident, Carl found himself grappling with a profound sense of inadequacy. He began to believe that he was not the talented director he once was; instead, he felt like a shadow of his former self, a man unrecognizable even to himself. This negative appraisal led him to adopt maladaptive strategies, as he felt that if he avoided challenging situations, he could protect himself from further confirming his fears of inadequacy. Carl's belief that he was fragile and incapable of handling demanding situations made avoidance feel like the only rational choice; he was convinced that stepping into the fray would only expose his perceived inadequacies. Each time he chose to steer clear of demanding tasks, he felt a quiet confirmation of his belief that he was incapable, reinforcing the idea that he was fragile and needed to avoid situations that could expose his perceived limitations. This negative self-appraisal led him to feel that he had to avoid situations that might expose his perceived inadequacies, as engaging with his work felt too risky and likely to confirm his worst fears about his abilities. This negative self-appraisal seeped into his daily life, making it difficult for him to cope with the pressures of his profession. Believing that he had lost his touch, Carl felt that every project he approached was a potential failure, heightening his sense of threat as he anticipated the inevitable exposure of his inadequacies. This negative self-appraisal intensified his sense of threat, as he walked into every new opportunity braced for the confirmation of his fears, convinced that failure was lurking just beneath the surface. Carl began to feel that he needed to distract himself from these feelings of inadequacy, leading him to immerse himself in work as a way to cope, despite knowing deep down that it was merely a temporary escape from his struggles. He started avoiding situations that reminded him of the event, such as filming in locations that were dimly lit or noisy, fearing that the reminder of that day would collapse him back into the paralyzing fear he had felt when the rig fell. By consistently steering clear of these reminders, he was left with the impression that the world was indeed a dangerous place, and he was incapable of handling it without retreating into his safe spaces. Each time he opted for safer, less demanding environments, he felt a twinge of guilt, reinforcing his belief that he was a lousy coper, someone who could not handle the realities of his job.

As he distanced himself from the chaos of his work, Carl noticed an increase in his hypervigilance. The world felt fraught with danger, and he found himself on high alert, especially at the sound of unexpected noises. The creaking of his old studio building or the sudden crash of a falling object would send him into a state of panic, causing him to jump and react with an intensity that startled even his closest colleagues. It was as if every sound was a potential threat, a reminder of his brush with death. This perception was rooted in the memories that replayed in his mind, creating a sense of immediacy in the danger he felt, as if the chaos of that day was still unfolding around him. This constant state of alertness only deepened his sense of inadequacy and isolation. Each time he turned to avoidance strategies, he inadvertently reinforced his belief that he was fragile, as it became clear to him that he could not face the world without these protective measures. His avoidance behaviors kept him from experiencing any evidence that the world might not be as dangerous as he feared, ensuring that his sense of threat remained as potent as it was on the day of the accident. The more he felt threatened by ordinary sounds, the more he leaned on avoidance strategies to cope, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place where he could not function properly. His reliance on these avoidance behaviors only deepened his sense of threat, as he never stayed in situations long enough to discover that they might not be as dangerous as he feared. The more he felt threatened by ordinary sounds, the more he retreated into himself, convinced that he was losing his grip on reality.

Carl also developed a tendency to distract himself from his memories through work, immersing himself in scripts and projects that demanded his attention. Yet, this maladaptive strategy only served to reinforce his negative appraisals. While he appeared to be engaged with his work outwardly, internally he was struggling, feeling that he was merely running from his past rather than confronting it. Each time he chose to immerse himself in work instead of confronting his memories, it further solidified his negative self-perception, making him feel more fragile and incapable of facing the realities of his trauma. Each distraction became a coping mechanism that reinforced his belief that he was unfit for his craft, further alienating him from colleagues who had once been his support system. In avoiding uncomfortable thoughts and feelings, Carl discovered that each act of diversion only confirmed his negative self-image, as he felt more and more detached from the director he once was. As he leaned on these maladaptive strategies, he began to internalize a sense of fragility, convinced that his need to avoid confronting his past validated his belief that he was incapable of handling the demands of his work. 

With time, Carl's avoidance behaviors led to a disconnection from his craft. He felt unqualified to direct, believing that he could no longer produce the same quality of work he once did. As he avoided projects that would put him in vulnerable situations, he became increasingly aware of how these choices were rooted in the memories of that fateful day. This avoidance kept the memories fresh and potent, making it difficult for him to confront his past, leaving him trapped in a cycle where the threat from those memories remained just as vivid and paralyzing as the day of the accident. This pattern of avoidance solidified his belief that he could not cope with the demands of his profession, further entrenching a negative view of himself and his abilities. His vivid recollections of fear and chaos turned into a lens through which he viewed his current reality, a reality that felt increasingly threatening and unmanageable. Each time he recalled the event, it was accompanied by a sinking realization that he was not only haunted by what had happened but also by the feeling that he was uniquely unprepared to handle similar situations in the future. As he continued to avoid situations that reminded him of the accident, he found that his sense of threat only escalated, as if each act of avoidance affirmed to him that the world was indeed unsafe. Despite his best efforts to avoid situations that triggered his memories, he realized that the more he tried to escape, the more entrenched he became in a cycle of fear and self-doubt. This cycle of avoidance created a self-fulfilling prophecy, as each escape reinforced his belief that he could not endure the world without retreating, solidifying the notion that danger was omnipresent.

Now seeking help, Carl is at a crossroads. He is motivated by a flicker of hope that he might reclaim the parts of himself he has lost, yet he remains terrified of revisiting his trauma. He longs to understand the "why" behind the accident and its aftermath, fearing that confronting those memories may expose him to the very vulnerabilities he has been running from. As he prepares to embark on this journey in therapy, Carl knows he has to confront the complex interplay of his memories, his feelings of threat, and the negative self-perceptions that have held him captive for far too long.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not explicitly convey how negative appraisals drive the use of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not clearly show how memories lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette lacks a direct connection indicating how memories result in negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: There is no clear depiction of how maladaptive strategies reinforce negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not illustrate how maladaptive strategies contribute to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Carl, a 52-year-old film director, had always been known for his ability to create compelling narratives, but his own life had taken a dark turn after a life-threatening accident that had left him feeling as though he were living in a story he no longer recognized. The incident occurred during a routine shoot in a remote location; while setting up a scene, an equipment malfunction caused a heavy rig to fall, narrowly missing him but injuring one of his crew members. The shock and fear of that moment had ingrained itself deeply in his mind, manifesting in vivid, haunting memories that replayed like a poorly edited film reel, filled with images of panic and chaos. Once these memories surfaced, they heightened his sense of threat, making him feel as though the chaos of that day was still a looming presence in his life. Once these memories surfaced, they transformed into a looming sense of threat, as Carl could not shake the feeling that the danger of that day had re-emerged, as if the chaos were still present in his life. These memories were so clear that he often found himself unable to articulate the emotions attached to them, trapped in a cycle where words failed him, leaving him feeling isolated in his anguish. Once these memories surfaced, they transformed into a looming sense of threat, as Carl could not shake the feeling that the danger of that day had re-emerged, as if the chaos were still present in his life.

In the months following the accident, Carl found himself grappling with a profound sense of inadequacy. He began to believe that he was not the talented director he once was; instead, he felt like a shadow of his former self, a man unrecognizable even to himself. This negative appraisal led him to adopt maladaptive strategies, as he felt that if he avoided challenging situations, he could protect himself from further confirming his fears of inadequacy. This negative self-appraisal led him to feel that he had to avoid situations that might expose his perceived inadequacies, as engaging with his work felt too risky and likely to confirm his worst fears about his abilities. This negative self-appraisal seeped into his daily life, making it difficult for him to cope with the pressures of his profession. Carl began to feel that he needed to distract himself from these feelings of inadequacy, leading him to immerse himself in work as a way to cope, despite knowing deep down that it was merely a temporary escape from his struggles. He started avoiding situations that reminded him of the event, such as filming in locations that were dimly lit or noisy, fearing that the reminder of that day would collapse him back into the paralyzing fear he had felt when the rig fell. By consistently steering clear of these reminders, he was left with the impression that the world was indeed a dangerous place, and he was incapable of handling it without retreating into his safe spaces. Each time he opted for safer, less demanding environments, he felt a twinge of guilt, reinforcing his belief that he was a lousy coper, someone who could not handle the realities of his job.

As he distanced himself from the chaos of his work, Carl noticed an increase in his hypervigilance. The world felt fraught with danger, and he found himself on high alert, especially at the sound of unexpected noises. The creaking of his old studio building or the sudden crash of a falling object would send him into a state of panic, causing him to jump and react with an intensity that startled even his closest colleagues. It was as if every sound was a potential threat, a reminder of his brush with death. This constant state of alertness only deepened his sense of inadequacy and isolation. Each time he turned to avoidance strategies, he inadvertently reinforced his belief that he was fragile, as it became clear to him that he could not face the world without these protective measures. The more he felt threatened by ordinary sounds, the more he leaned on avoidance strategies to cope, reinforcing his belief that the world was a dangerous place where he could not function properly. His reliance on these avoidance behaviors only deepened his sense of threat, as he never stayed in situations long enough to discover that they might not be as dangerous as he feared. The more he felt threatened by ordinary sounds, the more he retreated into himself, convinced that he was losing his grip on reality.

Carl also developed a tendency to distract himself from his memories through work, immersing himself in scripts and projects that demanded his attention. Yet, this maladaptive strategy only served to reinforce his negative appraisals. While he appeared to be engaged with his work outwardly, internally he was struggling, feeling that he was merely running from his past rather than confronting it. Each time he chose to immerse himself in work instead of confronting his memories, it further solidified his negative self-perception, making him feel more fragile and incapable of facing the realities of his trauma. Each distraction became a coping mechanism that reinforced his belief that he was unfit for his craft, further alienating him from colleagues who had once been his support system. As he leaned on these maladaptive strategies, he began to internalize a sense of fragility, convinced that his need to avoid confronting his past validated his belief that he was incapable of handling the demands of his work. 

With time, Carl's avoidance behaviors led to a disconnection from his craft. He felt unqualified to direct, believing that he could no longer produce the same quality of work he once did. As he avoided projects that would put him in vulnerable situations, he became increasingly aware of how these choices were rooted in the memories of that fateful day. This pattern of avoidance solidified his belief that he could not cope with the demands of his profession, further entrenching a negative view of himself and his abilities. His vivid recollections of fear and chaos turned into a lens through which he viewed his current reality, a reality that felt increasingly threatening and unmanageable. As he continued to avoid situations that reminded him of the accident, he found that his sense of threat only escalated, as if each act of avoidance affirmed to him that the world was indeed unsafe. Despite his best efforts to avoid situations that triggered his memories, he realized that the more he tried to escape, the more entrenched he became in a cycle of fear and self-doubt.

Now seeking help, Carl is at a crossroads. He is motivated by a flicker of hope that he might reclaim the parts of himself he has lost, yet he remains terrified of revisiting his trauma. He longs to understand the "why" behind the accident and its aftermath, fearing that confronting those memories may expose him to the very vulnerabilities he has been running from. As he prepares to embark on this journey in therapy, Carl knows he has to confront the complex interplay of his memories, his feelings of threat, and the negative self-perceptions that have held him captive for far too long.
